cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 3 (The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey): Fill the two-column chart: What he wrote about / why the journey was hard.
Chapter 10 (Palestine and Acre): Complete the timeline (1142, 1184, 1187).
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can find specific, predictable information in simple everyday material such as advertisements, prospectuses, menus, reference lists and timetables.
practice: Chapter 4 (Across the Mediterranean): First listening: Trace the route with a finger on the map.
Chapter 10 (Palestine and Acre): Complete the timeline (1142, 1184, 1187).
Whole book: the journey map and the Places & People cards.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 2 (A Young Scholar from Granada): Write one sentence about Ibn Jubayr’s job.
Chapter 10 (Palestine and Acre): Write one sentence with to + verb about Ibn Jubayr.
Language Review, “Use: My Travel Diary”: Write 4–5 diary sentences about a trip. Tell a partner first.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 2 (A Young Scholar from Granada): Say three sentences about your own dreams and goals with to + verb.
Chapter 9 (Damascus and Its Great Mosque): Describe your school building with a list.
Language Review, “Use: My Travel Diary”: Write 4–5 diary sentences about a trip. Tell a partner first.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Follow the route from Granada to Ceuta, across the sea, to Alexandria and on to Cairo.
lookFor: Instruction: Trace the route on the map while you listen. Then, with your partner, write one fact for each stop.
Check questions: What do you do while you listen? (trace the route) / How many facts for each stop? (one)
While learners work: Check the order of the stops. Check that pairs give the reason for the sea route. Listen for while + was/were + -ing and First, Then, Finally.
Evidence of “Route in order”: Orders the stops correctly.

peerObservation.chapter: Chapter 9: Damascus and Its Great Mosque
peerObservation.focus: List parts of the Great Mosque of Damascus that Ibn Jubayr describes.
lookFor: Instruction: With your partner, make a word web for the mosque. Match each part with its picture.
Check questions: What do you make? (a word web) / What do you match? (each part with its picture)
While learners work: Check that four parts are named from the text. Check that pairs explain why the description matters. Listen for could + base verb.
Evidence of “Mosque parts”: Names parts of the mosque from the text.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the A2 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the A2 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 3: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Explain what the Rihla is and why it made Ibn Jubayr famous”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 5 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 6, did you ask “What do you underline?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 13, how many learners were secure on “Later life facts”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?
When you asked “Which Turkish cities have historic hamams (Bursa, İstanbul, Konya)?” in Chapter 8, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?
Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 10 did you hear (*for thank · *nearly of two weeks)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners use the past continuous with while / when for a background action (Chapter 4) when they tell a travel story?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 4 route task, count learners who write one correct while + was/were + -ing sentence.
Recycle: in Chapters 11 and 12, ask for one travel sentence with a background action and a sudden event.
Check: after the A2 End-of-Level Test, note item 14 (past continuous with when) for the class in Score a test.
Decide: compare the counts and choose one story from the book to retell in the next lesson for more practice.

collaboration: Plan the Chapter 1 and Chapter 5 lessons (Al-Andalus, Saladin's hospital) with the history teacher, so learners meet the same facts in both lessons.
Share the travel safety tips from Chapter 12 with the geography teacher and compare the routes on a map together.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: Al-Andalus and a Great Traveler
objectives: I can say what Al-Andalus was.
I can say three facts about cities in Al-Andalus.
I can use because, because of and so.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Match four verbs with their past forms: build → built, take → took, bring → brought, have → had. Then complete three sentences with because of, so and because. Because of comes before a noun; because comes before a sentence; so gives the result.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the names: al-AN-da-lus, va-LEN-ci-a, gra-NA-da, COR-do-ba. Say the big number: Seven hundred thousand.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Where is this city? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 4 again. Find four cities and one number for each.
discussionPoints: In Al-Andalus, different people worked and studied together. How do people from different places work together in your school or town?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Living Side by Side” and “A City Rich in Learning”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 4. Find each city name and read the words after it. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a big city in three sentences with a fact, because of and so.

whatToNotice: Al-Andalus is the name of a land, not a city. Muslims ruled parts of Spain and Portugal from 711 to 1492.
Look at “Al-Andalus was in Europe because of its location …”. Because of comes before a noun.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Where is this city?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 4 again. Find four cities and one number for each.
Tap the picture hotspots “Living Side by Side” and “A City Rich in Learning”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find three groups of people who lived side by side.
Paragraph 3: find why people traveled a lot.
Paragraph 4: find where and when Ibn Jubayr was born.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: traded, location, learning, rural, bathhouses, thinker, holy, traveler.
“They often worked, traded and studied together.” What did they buy and sell?
Write one sentence: My town is famous because of its ….
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match three cities with three facts. All the facts are in paragraph 4.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find each city name and read the words after it.
selfCheck: Can I say what Al-Andalus was?
Can I say where Ibn Jubayr was born?
Can I say one sentence with because of?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a big city in three sentences with a fact, because of and so.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Close the book. Say three sentences about Al-Andalus from your notes. Then check one number in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Valencia is a famous city in the east of Spain, near the sea.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what Al-Andalus was.

thinkAloud.sentence: Sevilla was also a big city with 500 bathhouses and 1,000 mosques.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I see a busy city with many domes and minarets. There are hundreds of bathhouses and people everywhere in the streets. Close your eyes and add one more detail from the text.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “and often worked, traded and studied together.”
stopAndCheck.question: Who lived side by side in Al-Andalus? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.reflectionPrompt: In Al-Andalus, different people worked and studied together. How do people from different places work together in your school or town?

content.chapter: Chapter 2: A Young Scholar from Granada
objectives: I can say what Ibn Jubayr studied and what job he had.
I can name the goals of his journey.
I can use to + verb for dreams and goals.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Read two When sentences and say what When tells us (a time). Then complete the goals with to go, to gain and to get.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: SEC-re-tar-y, GOV-er-nor. Say KNOWL-edge without the k. Say “to go” quickly: /tə ɡəʊ/.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What is he doing? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 5 again. Find three goals.
discussionPoints: Ibn Jubayr wanted to learn new things on his journey. What do you want to learn this year?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “A Good Education” and “Work in Granada”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 5. Find the words “biggest dreams”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Say three sentences about your own dreams: “One of my biggest dreams is to …”.

whatToNotice: The chapter starts with three great travelers: Ibn Jubayr, Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.
Then it moves from young Ibn Jubayr to the man who started a journey in 1183.
Look at “One of his biggest dreams was to go on Hajj.” After dream and goal, we use to + verb.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What is he doing?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 5 again. Find three goals.
Tap the picture hotspots “A Good Education” and “Work in Granada”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraphs 2–3: find how far each traveler went.
Paragraph 5: find what he studied and his job.
Paragraph 6: find how old he was when the journey started.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: come to mind, further, gain new knowledge.
“He also wanted to gain new knowledge and skills during his journey to Mecca.” What did he want to learn?
Write one sentence: When I grow up, I want to be ….
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose his biggest dream. Read paragraph 5 before you answer.
selfCheck: Can I say what he studied?
Can I say his job?
Can I say one dream of mine with to + verb?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Say three sentences about your own dreams: “One of my biggest dreams is to …”.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Compare the three travelers in three sentences.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “He had a good education.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why Ibn Jubayr wanted to travel.

thinkAloud.sentence: Ibn Jubayr traveled less, but he was one of the first great travelers because he wrote one of the first travel books.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: Why was he a great traveler if he traveled less? The word “because” gives the reason: he wrote one of the first travel books. Find one more reason in the chapter and say it with “because”.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “He went much further than the other two travelers.”
stopAndCheck.question: Which traveler went the furthest? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.reflectionPrompt: Ibn Jubayr wanted to learn new things on his journey. What do you want to learn this year?

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Rihla and a Dangerous Journey
objectives: I can say what the Rihla is.
I can say why the journey was difficult.
I can use almost, by and on foot.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “almost every day” means (nearly every day). Then complete the sentence with by and on.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: TRAV-el DI-a-ry, de-SCRIBES, PRIS-on-ers. Say the chunks: by BOAT, by CAM-el, on FOOT.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What is he writing? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 3 again. Find how long the journey took.
discussionPoints: Ibn Jubayr wrote almost every day. What would you write about your day today?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “A Travel Diary” and “By Boat, Camel and Foot”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Find the words “almost every day”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Tell how you traveled on a real trip with by and on foot.

whatToNotice: Rihla means travel book. His book became a model for other travel books.
Look at “He traveled by boat, by camel, and on foot …”. For walking, we say on foot.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What is he writing?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 3 again. Find how long the journey took.
Tap the picture hotspots “A Travel Diary” and “By Boat, Camel and Foot”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what the word rihla means.
Paragraph 2: find when he wrote in his diary.
Paragraph 3: find three ways he traveled.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: trip, travel diary, describes, sights, Crusaders, prisoners, slaves, war zone.
“Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey.” What does a travel diary have in it?
Write one sentence in a travel diary about today.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will read a sentence about when he wrote. Is it true or false? Read paragraph 2.
selfCheck: Can I say what the Rihla is?
Can I say why the journey was dangerous?
Can I say how he traveled?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Tell how you traveled on a real trip with by and on foot.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Say three sentences about the Rihla.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Ibn Jubayr wrote a travel diary about his journey.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what the Rihla is.

thinkAloud.strategy: Guess a word from its sentence
thinkAloud.sentence: In the Arabic language, the word rihla means travel book.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I do not know “Rihla”. The next sentence explains it: In Arabic, rihla means travel book. Do the same with another new word in the paragraph.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “while he still remembered the details.”
stopAndCheck.question: When did Ibn Jubayr write in his diary? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.reflectionPrompt: Ibn Jubayr wrote almost every day. What would you write about your day today?

objectives: I can follow the route from Granada to Alexandria.
I can say why he traveled by sea.
I can use While, After, Then and finally.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Say which action was longer: The sailing or the storm. Then complete While, After, Then and finally in the route sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the places: SEU-ta, sar-DIN-i-a, SIC-i-ly, al-ex-AN-dri-a. Say ROUTE like “root”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the route on a map. Read paragraphs 1 and 2 again. Find the dates.
discussionPoints: The storm was terrible, but the ship continued. What helps you continue when something is difficult?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “A Terrible Storm” and “A Famous Lighthouse”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraphs 1 and 2. Look for There, While, After and finally. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Retell his route, then your route to school, with First, Then and Finally.

whatToNotice: The chapter is a route: Granada, Ceuta, the islands, Crete, Alexandria, then Cairo.
Look at “While they were sailing …, a terrible storm caught them.” The sailing was the longer action.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What can you see?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the route on a map.
Read paragraphs 1 and 2 again. Find the dates.
Tap the picture hotspots “A Terrible Storm” and “A Famous Lighthouse”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what he saw near Sardinia.
Paragraph 2: find where the storm caught the ship and why he traveled by sea.
Paragraph 3: find who stopped the Christian soldiers.
Paragraph 4: find what amazed him in Alexandria.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: got off, managed to, amazed.
“The very big size and beauty of the lighthouse amazed him.” Was he surprised in a good way?
Write one sentence: … amazed me.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put four events in order. Read paragraphs 1 and 2 from the beginning.
wrongAnswerSupport: Look for There, While, After and finally.
selfCheck: Can I name the stops in order?
Can I say why he went by sea?
Can I use While and After?

noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Say the route in four sentences.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “At that time, traveling by sea was faster and safer than traveling by land.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how Ibn Jubayr crossed the Mediterranean.

thinkAloud.sentence: That’s why Ibn Jubayr followed this interesting route.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “That’s why” points back to the sentence before: Traveling by sea was faster and safer than by land. That is the reason for his route. Find one more reason in the chapter and say it with “because”.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “a terrible storm caught them.”
stopAndCheck.question: What happened between the islands? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can say what Ibn Jubayr saw in Cairo.
I can say why he respected Saladin.
I can use so … that, did not and could.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Say what “so safe that …” shows. Then choose the right form after did not, used it and could.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: PRAISED, un-der con-STRUC-tion, PYR-a-mids, NI-lom-e-ter. Say “two thousand loaves of bread”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. What is the big building over the river? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read paragraph 2 again. Find three good things Saladin did.
discussionPoints: Saladin helped poor people, students and sick people. Who helps people in your town?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “A High Bridge” and “The Nilometer”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Find the word “so” after “very high”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a good leader in three sentences.

whatToNotice: This chapter has many facts. Read one paragraph at a time.
Look at “The roads were also so safe that people could travel day and night …”. So … that gives a result.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. What is the big building over the river?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read paragraph 2 again. Find three good things Saladin did.
Tap the picture hotspots “A High Bridge” and “The Nilometer”.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find the name of the state and its ruler.
Paragraph 3: find why the bridge was very high.
Paragraph 4: find what was special about the hospital.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: felt great respect, praised, mosque, fair rules, fear, noticed, enemy attacks, under construction, floods, separate, special care, pyramids, measure, guesthouses, public baths, take care of sick people, giving out, loaves.
“… a very large bridge under construction …” Was the bridge finished?
Write one sentence with praised.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose why the bridge was high. Read paragraph 3.
selfCheck: Can I name three places in Cairo?
Can I give two reasons why he respected Saladin?
Can I use did not + base verb?

noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Say four good things Saladin did.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “It was completely free.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what Ibn Jubayr saw in Cairo.

thinkAloud.sentence: He did not ask the farmers to pay the Nile water taxes.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: Who is “He”? The sentence before is about Saladin’s fair rules, so “He” is Saladin. Find one more he, she or they and say who it is.

stopAndCheck.question: Who was the ruler of Cairo? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can say what a caravan is.
I can say how you could see rich and poor travelers.
I can use be like.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Choose what “were like” means. Then complete the sentences with who, needed and were.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: CAR-a-van, ROY-al, MOV-ing PAL-a-ces.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the picture first. Say three things you see. Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read it again and find the comparison with like.
discussionPoints: In the caravan, rich and poor people traveled together. How can we make everyone feel welcome in a group?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “Moving Palaces” and “A Long Line of Camels”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again. Find the words “You only needed to look at …”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe the chapter picture with “It looks like …”.

whatToNotice: This is a short chapter with one big picture: A camel caravan in the desert.
Look at “They were like beautiful moving palaces.” The tents were not palaces; they were like palaces.
readListen: Look at the picture first. Say three things you see.
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read it again and find the comparison with like.
Tap the picture hotspots “Moving Palaces” and “A Long Line of Camels”.
findAnswerInStory: Find where the caravan was going.
Find what you needed to look at.
Find what the tents of royal people were like.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: tents, moving palaces, caravan.
“The tents of rich royal people were amazing.” Why are they called moving palaces?
Write one sentence with is like.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will read a sentence about rich and poor travelers. Is it true or false?
wrongAnswerSupport: Find the words “You only needed to look at …”.
selfCheck: Can I say what a caravan is?
Can I say how to see who was rich?

mediationTasks.translation: Write “They were like beautiful moving palaces.” in your home language.

thinkAloud.sentence: The tents of rich royal people were amazing.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I see a long line of camels in the desert. Some tents are small and simple. The tents of rich people are big and beautiful, like palaces on the move. Close your eyes and add one more detail from the text.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “You only needed to look at their tents.”
stopAndCheck.question: How could you see who was rich and who was poor? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can say when Ibn Jubayr arrived in Mecca and how long he stayed.
I can explain why he compares Mecca to a mother’s body.
I can use can, cannot, with respect and such as.
content.pedagogy: Look, listen and read first. Then find the answer sentences, do the Quick Challenge, and use the chapter’s Language Focus.
content.grammarFocus: Say what can and cannot show. Then complete with, such as and surprisingly.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say the stress: NAR-row, MIR-a-cles, GI-ant. Say can weakly /kən/ and cannot clearly.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the title and the picture. Where is he? Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes. Read the quotation slowly. Imagine the narrow valley and the big crowd.
discussionPoints: Ibn Jubayr describes the holy places with respect. How do you show respect in a special place?
interactiveTips: Tap the picture hotspots “The Holy Ka’bah” and “Hills around Mecca”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the quotation again. Find “narrow valley” and “a very big crowd”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a special place with “is located in” and “can”.

whatToNotice: The chapter has Ibn Jubayr’s own words in quotation marks.
Look at “… it can get bigger and have space for a very big crowd of people.” Can shows that something is possible.
readListen: Look at the title and the picture. Where is he?
Listen to the chapter once. Follow the text with your eyes.
Read the quotation slowly. Imagine the narrow valley and the big crowd.
Tap the picture hotspots “The Holy Ka’bah” and “Hills around Mecca”.
findAnswerInStory: Find the month and the year he arrived.
Find the countries people came from.
Find what a mother’s body does.

metadata.title: Ibn Jubayr A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of the traveler Ibn Jubayr at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of Ibn Jubayr’s journey.
Follow his route from Al-Andalus to Mecca and back.
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen or read first, then check.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One place on Ibn Jubayr’s journey I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 13 chapters. Make a small plan before Chapter 1. A plan helps you keep going.
points: Choose your days. For example: two chapters a week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one goal for this book: “At the end, I want to …”.
Save new words to My words. Review them after one day, after three days and after one week.
Before Chapter 1, open section 10, “Look Back”, and answer the “I can” questions.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read one paragraph at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Listen first when audio is available, then read.
points: First time: Listen or read for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 4. Follow the Route
sections.text: Ibn Jubayr traveled from Granada to Mecca and back. Keep a small route list in your notebook.
points: Write each new place.
Add one fact for each place.
Use the route to retell the story.

sections.title: 5. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Tap the two hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 6. Quick Challenge and Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge and three Language Focus activities.
points: Answer first, then read the feedback.
Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence and try again.
Activity 1: look. Activity 2: practise. Activity 3: use the language about your own life.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and numbers. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Write the names and numbers in a list.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: Ibn Jubayr’s journey shows respect, patience, helpfulness and love of learning. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Respect: Different people lived side by side (Chapter 1).
Kindness and fairness: Saladin helped poor and sick people (Chapter 5).
Patience: He waited for good winds (Chapter 10).
Helpfulness: A king helped the passengers (Chapter 11).
Learning: Travel and look for knowledge (Chapter 13).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these questions before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge. For each one, say: not yet, a little or yes. They come from the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2020) for level A2. One book is one step, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can understand short narratives and descriptions of someone’s life composed in simple language.”
Speaking: “I can tell a story or describe something in a simple list of points.”
Writing: “I can produce a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like ‘and’, ‘but’ and ‘because’.”
Mediation: “I can convey the main point(s) involved in short, simple texts on everyday subjects of immediate interest, provided these are expressed clearly in simple language.”
What helped me most in this book?
What was hard, and what did I do about it?
What will I do in a different way in my next book?
